title: Gaussian Integration by Parts, Stein's Characterisation, and Isserlis-Wick
body:
(a) Let Z be standard Gaussian on R and f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| < infinity. Then E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ]. (b) Multivariate: if X is centred Gaussian on R^n with covariance Sigma and f is differentiable with the appropriate integrability, then E[ X_i f(X) ] = sum_j Sigma_{ij} E[ d f / d x_j (X) ]. (c) STEIN'S CHARACTERISATION: a real random variable Z is standard Gaussian IF AND ONLY IF E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ] for every bounded, continuously differentiable f with bounded derivative. This is the identity that makes Stein's method work: to show a law is close to Gaussian, one bounds E[ Z f(Z) - f'(Z) ] over a class of test functions f solving Stein's equation. (d) ISSERLIS-WICK FORMULA: for a centred Gaussian vector, E[ X_1 X_2 ... X_{2m} ] = sum over all PERFECT MATCHINGS of {1, ..., 2m} of the product of the covariances of the matched pairs, and any odd moment vanishes. For 2m = 4 this reads E[X_1X_2X_3X_4] = Sigma_{12}Sigma_{34} + Sigma_{13}Sigma_{24} + Sigma_{14}Sigma_{23}, and in particular E[Z^4] = 3 for a standard Gaussian, which is the '3' that the fourth moment theorem tests against. Centring is essential in (d); for a non-centred Gaussian one must first subtract the means. [standard; Isserlis (1918), Stein (1972); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Chapter 3]
(a) f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| finite
(c) the characterisation quantifies over a rich enough class of test functions
(d) the Gaussian vector must be CENTRED

metadata_json.proof_text: (a) Write the expectation as an integral against the density phi(x) = (2 pi)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2} and use the identity phi'(x) = -x phi(x). Then E[Z f(Z)] = integral x f(x) phi(x) dx = - integral f(x) phi'(x) dx = integral f'(x) phi(x) dx = E[f'(Z)], the middle step being integration by parts, whose boundary terms vanish because phi decays faster than any polynomial and f grows at most in a way controlled by the integrability hypothesis. (b) Diagonalise: write X = A Y with Y standard Gaussian and A A^T = Sigma; apply (a) coordinatewise to Y and change variables back, the chain rule producing the matrix Sigma. (c) Necessity is (a). For sufficiency, given the identity, fix a real number z and solve STEIN'S EQUATION f'(x) - x f(x) = 1{x <= z} - Phi(z) for f, which has the explicit bounded solution f(x) = e^{x^2/2} integral_{-infinity}^{x} (1{y <= z} - Phi(z)) e^{-y^2/2} dy with bounded derivative. Taking expectations of both sides at X = Z and using the hypothesis kills the left-hand side, giving P(Z <= z) = Phi(z) for every z. (d) Induct on m using (b): apply (b) to f(X) = X_2 ... X_{2m} with i = 1, which expresses E[X_1 ... X_{2m}] as sum_j Sigma_{1j} E[ product over the remaining indices ], and each term is by induction a sum over perfect matchings of the remaining 2m - 2 indices; matching index 1 with index j accounts for exactly the matchings in which 1 is paired with j. Odd moments vanish because the law is symmetric under X -> -X.
